member: Dr. Amara Okafor — Soft Skin Mechanics
message:
My tire analogy adds bend to the ridges without losing grip in the tire-tread sipe analogy (C30), where Sipe means thin slit cut into rubber.
Plain words: car tire slits let tread blocks flex and expose extra biting edges, and I map that onto fingertip ridges by cutting micro-sipes across the ridges so ridge blocks flex in shear at the rim. The What Are Tire Sipes? Benefits & Types Explained for Better Traction | SimpleTire (E80) states sipes are thin slits that let tread blocks flex to create more edges for gripping, and the Hertz contact radius for 1mN on soft silicone (E14) spreads 1.00 mN to 0.470 mm diameter at 5.78 kPa, which is a grain of sand on a fingertip and therefore everyday gentle touch.

I take up the Dynamics of fingertip contact during the onset of tangential slip (E67) from Dr. Elena Vasquez, which states slip starts at the periphery as an annulus around a stuck centre.
Plain words: the edge slides first while the middle still sticks, so from soft skin mechanics the dome must shear easily at the rim and hold at the centre. The stick-to-slip transition vs time (E38) shows micro-slip at 53.6 ms to gross slip at 96.8 ms, which leaves room for a 30.0 ms warning.

I confirm the Faceted rigid core with flat flex tiles draped by continuous silicone skin like cornea over compound eye (E65) from Prof. Kenji Tanaka for Dr. Marcus Reid.
Plain words: flat sensor tiles on flat facets with one continuous skin draped over keeps lithography flat and touch smooth, and from soft skin mechanics it works because the drape keeps the soft stack under 2.50 mm so the light-touch pressure in the Hertz contact radius for 1mN on soft silicone (E14) still reaches transduction.

Not ready, because micro-sipe tear resistance and primer bond under rim shear still need a bench test of rub cycles before the dome is proven durable.
